blocks.content: The Governor is an integral part of the State Legislature and possesses significant legislative powers including the authority to promulgate ordinances when the legislature is not in session.

rows: Promulgates ordinances on subjects in the State and Concurrent Lists
Promulgates ordinances on subjects in the Union and Concurrent Lists
Requires President's instructions for certain specific bills before promulgation
Does not require prior instructions from any outside authority
Includes 'Cooperative Movement' along with Art, Science, Literature, and Social Service
Excludes 'Cooperative Movement' for Rajya Sabha nominations

items: Cooperative movement is an additional category for nominations to the Legislative Council by the Governor, which is not present in the President's nomination criteria for Rajya Sabha.
Reservation of a High Court-related bill for the President is mandatory, not discretionary, under Article 200.
An ordinance promulgated by the Governor ceases to operate 6 weeks from the date of reassembly of the State Legislature unless approved earlier.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Governor is an integral part of the State Legislature under Article 168, despite not being a member of either House.
Under Article 200, the Governor can give assent, withhold assent, return a non-money bill for reconsideration, or reserve a bill for the consideration of the President.
The Governor must reserve any bill that endangers the constitutional position of the State High Court for the President's assent.
Under Article 213, the Governor can promulgate ordinances when either or both Houses of the State Legislature are not in session.
The Governor nominates 1/6th of the total members of the State Legislative Council from persons having special knowledge in literature, science, art, cooperative movement, and social service.
